title: edge-tls-ticket-rotation-keepalive-thrash-incident-diary
content:
Summary

Short version: on 2029-10-07 we observed a P0 degradation of hosted API streaming endpoints (increased TTFB, intermittent 5xx for long-poll streams, large number of client reconnects). Root cause hypothesis: an edge TLS session-ticket rotation change in our CDN + an aggressive keepalive/TTL mismatch triggered repeated full TLS handshakes, amplifying connection churn which interacted poorly with the multiplexing scheduler and per-edge acceptor limits, causing ephemeral stream starvation and a cascade of backpressure into the serving runtime.

Impact
- Customer-facing: streaming responses intermittently stalled or required reconnect; p95 TTFB on streaming endpoints rose from ~60ms to ~1.2s during peak.
- Internal: surge of ephemeral connections exhausted acceptor queues on several edge instances in us-west-2 and eu-west-1, causing 502/524 errors from the edge for long-tail requests.
- Time window: first alert at 2029-10-07T09:13:42Z, mitigated initial by 2029-10-07T10:07:00Z, full stabilization by 2029-10-08T02:30:00Z after staged fixes and a config rollback.

Observed signals (raw)
- Spikes in TLS full-handshake rate: +6x baseline on edge nodes (TLS full handshakes per minute).
- Accept queue depth alerts triggered on edge fleet autoscaler: average accept backlog > 800 (threshold 200) for 20m.
- Multiplex scheduler reports: starvation warnings, stream create latency increased, per-connection stream-count estimation drifted.
- Hosted-api logs: increased client reset error codes: STREAM_RESET/ECONNRESET and edge-origin 502/524 entries.

What changed recently?
- CDN vendor rolled an edge config change (ticket rotation frequency bump) on 2029-10-07 08:55Z for security rollout.
- We had a recent edge-proxy release (edge-proxy v2.7.4) two days prior that adjusted keepalive probing heuristics to be more aggressive under low-traffic conditions (PR referenced in linked artifacts).
- Combination of the two: shorter ticket TTL + more aggressive keepalive caused clients and intermediate proxies to re-initiate connections more frequently and not reuse session tickets as expected.

Timeline (high level)
- 2029-10-07T08:55Z — CDN vendor config change deployed (ticket rotation frequency increased).
- 2029-10-07T09:11Z — first internal anomaly detection: streaming p95 increase and TLS handshake rate uplift in us-west-2. Pager triggered at 09:13.
- 09:21 — oncall triage: confirmed handshake spike, client reconnects rising.
- 09:30 — mitigation: temporarily increase edge acceptor pool and bump burst capacity in us-west-2 by 15%.
- 09:46 — partial improvement but persistent oscillation; further investigation shows multiplex scheduler failing to reclaim per-connection state quickly.
- 10:00 — roll back edge-proxy keepalive probing experiment on a canary subset; handshake rate drops on canary.
- 10:07 — CDN vendor agreed to revert ticket rotation change for our account while we investigate (mitigation controlled by vendor).
- 10:20 — system metrics trending back but residual 5xx until midnight for low-volume tails due to KV cache pressure and stream reassembly load.
- 2029-10-08T02:30Z — full fleet stabilized after KV cache GC tuning and acceptor throttles updated.

Root cause analysis (hypothesis chain)
1) External trigger: CDN ticket rotation shortened TLS session reuse window, causing more full-handshakes.
2) Internal change: edge-proxy keepalive heuristics were more aggressive, proactively probing/closing idle TCP connections; in combination this made connection churn worse.
3) Multiplex scheduler and acceptor limits: scheduler was using a moving-average estimator for active streams per-conn that under-estimated transient increases in stream churn, leading to delayed reallocation of worker capacity and queue buildup.
4) KV cache pressure: repeated reconnections increased KV cache lookup/eviction churn on mindchain layer leading to extra CPU and GC pauses, amplifying tail latency and causing some streaming sessions to time out and return 524/502.

Why did the acceptor queues fill?
- Edge node TCP stacks saw a burst of SYN+TLS inflight. Each new connection requires more CPU and worker assignment; our autoscaler scaled but with a lag, and acceptor pool sizes are configured assuming lower handshake rates.

What went well during response
- Detection: anomaly detection detected TTFB and handshake rate deviation quickly; pagers fired as expected.
- Cross-team coordination: SRE + Edge + CDN vendor + Runtime responded promptly, vendor reverted the config within ~12 minutes of our escalation.
- Canary rollback of edge-proxy probing was effective and gave a quick validation signal.

What could have gone better
- Observability gaps: we lacked a quick pivot view that correlates TLS full-handshakes, accept queue depth, and multiplex scheduler internal counters in one dashboard. Building that view would have shaved ~20m off triage.
- Runbook clarity: runbook for "edge-handshake-storm" exists but assumes vendor rollback is not an option; we need a branch for vendor-side misconfig rollbacks and a customer-facing comms template.
- Autoscaler tuning: acceptor autoscaler reaction time and step sizes were not tuned for handshake storms.

Immediate mitigations applied
- Ask CDN vendor to revert ticket rotation change for our account (accepted and applied at 10:07Z).
- Canary rollback of edge-proxy keepalive heuristics to previous stable config.
- Increase acceptor pool and temporary burst capacity on impacted edge rings.
- KV cache GC tuning: increased cache memory target and extended soft-eviction window to reduce thrash.

Longer-term fixes and action items (owner + ETA)
- SRE/Edge: add an "edge-handshake-storm" dashboard that correlates TLS handshake rate, acceptor queue depth, multiplexer stream-create latency, and KV cache eviction rate. (Owner: Riley Chen, ETA: 2029-10-21)
- Edge: revert keepalive probing default and gate the aggressive heuristic behind an explicit opt-in flag; add a canary gating step to the rollout checklist. (Owner: Marcus Feld, ETA: 2029-10-14)
- Platform: adopt an autoscaler policy for acceptor pools that can scale based on TLS handshake rate and SYN backlog, not just CPU. (Owner: Aisha Gomez, ETA: 2029-11-04)
- Runtime: fix multiplex scheduler estimator to be robust to short-term churn spikes (use EWMA with burst sensitivity) and add a scheduler health signal. (Owner: Priya Nair, ETA: 2029-11-11)
- Release ops: add vendor-change monitoring and a playbook for vendor-side parameter rollbacks + SLA for vendor communication. (Owner: Eng Ops, ETA: 2029-10-28)
- Customer comms: draft a post-incident note for customers using streaming endpoints explaining impact and mitigations. (Owner: CS, ETA: 2029-10-09)

Runbook draft: "edge-handshake-storm" (triage checklist)
- Step 0: Confirm scope — run query: edge_tls.handshake_rate{region,edge_ring} > 3x baseline for >5m. If false -> follow standard latency triage.
- Step 1: Check if TLS ticket rotation or CDN parameters changed recently: query vendor change log / contact vendor channel.
- Step 2: Check edge-proxy release history: kubectl get pods -l app=edge-proxy -n edge-prod; describe recent image rollouts and PRs.
- Step 3: If handshake rate is elevated, apply short-term mitigations in order: 1) Increase acceptor pool on impacted rings: curl -XPOST https://edge-ops/api/acceptors/scale -d '{"ring":"us-west-2","delta":+10}' 2) Bump burst capacity config for ring via infra console.
- Step 4: Canary revert edge-proxy keepalive flag on one ring and watch handshake trend for 10m. Command: kubectl set env deployment/edge-proxy EDGE_KEEPALIVE_AGGRESSIVE=false -n edge-prod; rollback if improvement seen.
- Step 5: If vendor-side change detected and vendor can revert, escalate using vendor playbook channel (Vendor Ops runbook).
- Step 6: If handshake storms persist: temporarily tighten acceptance policy for low-priority traffic (route to low-cost backend) to preserve capacity for streaming traffic.
- Step 7: Post-mitigations: collect heapdumps and pprof from edge-proxy and runtime nodes (see internal SRE debugging checklist).

Dry notes / open questions (investigation to complete)
- Why did some edge rings (ap-south-1) not see the same magnitude of effect? Hypothesis: different CDN pop behavior and client distribution, need to correlate client geographic mix.
- Did any customers with long-lived keepalive-adjacent proxies (corporate proxies) observe higher reconnects? Need to coordinate with CS to gather customer-side connection traces.
- KV cache telemetry: what exact keyspaces saw eviction uptick? correlate with namespace metrics.

Artifacts collected
- pcap snippets from affected edge node (saved to s3://ri-sre/incident/2029-10-07/pcap/)
- edge-proxy logs for impacted ring (s3 link)
- dashboard snapshots (included in linked_artifacts Slack thread)

Communication plan
- Internal: summary to eng-all and SRE channel by 2029-10-09 with timeline and action items.
- External/customers: CS to send targeted notify to affected accounts with suggested mitigations for client-side proxies (e.g., enable session ticket reuse), and public post-mortem after root cause confirmed.

Post-incident follow-ups (tracking board)
- Create JIRA-SRE-1412 with sub-tasks per action item above.
- Schedule a post-mortem working session (2 hours) with Edge, Runtime, Platform, and CS to finalize findings and decide permanent fixes (target: 2029-10-16).

Appendix: commands and quick checks
- Quick TLS handshake rate query (promql): sum(rate(tls_handshakes_total[1m])) by (edge_ring)
- Accept queue query: sum(rate(edge_accept_backlog[1m])) by (edge_ring)
- Check edge-proxy deployment: kubectl -n edge-prod get deploy edge-proxy -o yaml | egrep "image:|EDGE_KEEPALIVE_AGGRESSIVE"
- Revert env on canary: kubectl -n edge-prod set env deploy/edge-proxy EDGE_KEEPALIVE_AGGRESSIVE=false --record
- Collect pprof: curl http://$EDGE_NODE:6060/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30 -o /tmp/profile.pprof

Notes to self
- Keep this doc as the live incident diary until post-mortem completed. Save snapshots of dashboards as evidence.
- When writing final post-mortem, include simplified sequence diagram showing how ticket rotation -> handshake rate -> acceptor backlog -> scheduler starvation -> KV cache thrash produced the cascade.

End of diary (initial draft).
